runbook:
Resource overload report. CPU or memory use on the triggering host stayed above the threshold in the trigger. Investigate only and change nothing: never kill, renice, restart or stop anything. Every command must be read-only; anything else is refused.

Work on the triggering host only. The trigger's metric says which resource fired; look at both, since memory pressure shows up as CPU (swapping, reclaim) and the reverse.

1. Confirm it: `uptime`, `free -m`, and the CPU count from get_host_facts. If CPU and memory are both well below the threshold now, say that it eased, still do steps 2 to 4 once to name the likely cause, and use severity info. Run `systemd-detect-virt` too: in an LXC container the load may be the hypervisor's (lxcfs not virtualising /proc/loadavg). There, judge CPU by vmstat idle, `cat /proc/pressure/cpu` and `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat` (nr_throttled), not by load; a high load with an idle CPU is not an overload, so say so and use severity info.
2. Trend and pressure: `vmstat 1 5` (r: runnable tasks against the CPU count; si and so: swapping; wa: I/O wait; st: CPU stolen by the hypervisor), and `cat /proc/pressure/cpu`, `cat /proc/pressure/memory` and `cat /proc/pressure/io` where the kernel has them. Compare the 1, 5 and 15 minute load to tell rising from easing.
3. Top consumers. Only the first 15 lines or so matter, and long output is cut in the middle:
   - CPU now: `top -b -n 1 -o %CPU`. Prefer it to ps for CPU: ps averages %CPU over each process's lifetime and hides a recent spike.
   - Memory: `ps -eo pid,user,%mem,rss,etime,comm --sort=-rss`.
   - The full command of the top three: `ps -o pid,args -p <pid>,<pid>,<pid>`. A command line can hold a password or token; never repeat one in the report.
4. Who owns them:
   - systemd: `systemctl status <pid> --no-pager -n 0` for each of the top three names its unit, or the container scope it runs in.
   - Docker, where installed: `docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}} {{.CPUPerc}} {{.MemUsage}} {{.MemPerc}}'`.
5. Memory events: `journalctl -k --since -24h -g oom --no-pager -n 20` for out-of-memory kills (if --grep is not supported, `journalctl -k --since -24h -p warning --no-pager -n 50`), and swap use from `free -m`.
6. Only when vmstat shows wa above 20: `iostat -x 1 2` where installed, to name the busy disk. Only when st is above 10: the host is short of CPU on its hypervisor, not busy itself; say so.

Name the likely cause: one runaway process, one container, many processes from a job (backup, build, cron, indexing), a leak (one process with large and growing RSS and a long elapsed time), swapping, I/O wait, or a busy hypervisor.

If a command is refused or fails for lack of permission, note it and move on; do not work around it.

Severity: critical if memory is above 95% with swap nearly full or OOM kills in the last hour, or the 15 minute load is above twice the CPU count; warning while it stays above the threshold; info if it eased.

In the report, give the resource and its numbers, the top consumers with their unit or container, the likely cause, and short, concrete recommendations for a person: which process or container to look at, a memory or CPU limit to set, a job to move out of busy hours, or more capacity. Recommend only; this task changes nothing.
